nature-found-044.title: Economics: the science of running the world's household
nature-found-044.text: The word comes from the Ancient Greek oikonomia, the way to run a household. Economics is the social science that studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used. It looks at how economic agents, such as households, firms, buyers and sellers, behave and interact, and how whole economies work. The field was once called political economy. Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations, published in 1776, is described as the birth of economics as a separate discipline. Smith named land, labour and capital as the basic inputs of production, the subject of {{ref:nature-econ-086}}. A widely accepted definition came from Lionel Robbins in 1932. He called economics the study of human behaviour as a relationship between ends and scarce means that have alternative uses. Economists divide their field in two ways. One split is by scale: the study of individual agents and markets, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-134}}, versus the study of whole economies, covered in {{ref:nature-econ-541}}. The second includes growth, inflation and unemployment. The other separates positive economics, which describes what is, from normative economics, which argues for what ought to be. Controlled experiments are hard in economics, so theories are mostly tested on observed data, using statistical methods called econometrics. Economic analysis now reaches far beyond business, into law, politics and the environment.

nature-found-031.title: Externalities: costs and benefits that land on someone else
nature-found-031.text: Every car on the road pollutes the air, yet neither car makers nor drivers pay that cost to society. Economists call this an externality: a cost or benefit that falls on a third party who had no part in the activity that caused it. Externalities are the parts of production or consumption that carry no price. Pollution of the environment is the textbook example of a negative, or harmful, one. Because the market price does not reflect the true cost or benefit to society, resources could be better allocated. That makes externalities one cause of the problem explored in {{ref:nature-found-045}}, where a market loses value. Alfred Marshall first developed the idea in the 1890s, and Arthur Pigou brought it wider attention in the 1920s. Governments often try to "internalize" externalities, so that prices include all the costs and benefits. The most common tool is a tax on whoever causes them. Setting the right tax is hard, because regulators rarely have full information about the externality. The idea has spread beyond economics, into environmental science, public health and urban planning.

nature-found-045.title: Market failure: when free markets waste value
nature-found-045.text: Mainstream economics keeps a list of the ways free markets go wrong. Market failure is a situation in which a free market's allocation of goods and services is not efficient, so economic value is lost. The causes on the list include the power of a single dominant seller, externalities, and missing or unequal information. Others are one side's greater power to bargain, irrational behaviour, and unemployment or inflation. Another cause is goods that no one can be kept from enjoying, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-633}}. Economists who study the environment deal mostly with externalities. Governments respond in several ways. They often tax or restrict goods with negative externalities and subsidise goods with positive ones. Other remedies include rules based on weighing costs against benefits, or market tools that change incentives, such as emission fees or redefined rights of ownership. Most mainstream economists think government can sometimes improve the outcome, as with building codes or endangered species laws. But government interventions can themselves misallocate resources, a problem explored in {{ref:nature-found-064}}. Economists first used the term in 1958, though the idea is traced back to John Stuart Mill and Henry Sidgwick.

nature-found-030.title: Environmental economics: weighing what markets leave out
nature-found-030.text: Markets are often trusted to steer resources to good uses with no one in charge, through the combined effect of many self-interested choices. Environmental economists work where that steering cannot be relied on. Environmental economics is the branch of economics that studies environmental problems and the economic effects of policies meant to deal with them. Market failure, where markets do not put resources to their best use, is the idea at its centre. The field weighs the costs and benefits of policies on air pollution, water quality, toxic substances, solid waste and global warming. Most environmental economists are trained as economists and bring economic tools to these problems. Putting an economic value on the environment is a major topic, because many natural resources carry no market price at all. The name became popular in the 1960s. Yet links between economics and the environment go back to Condorcet, Adam Smith, Malthus and Ricardo. An economic solution to environmental problems proposed by Ronald Coase is credited with settling the field as a sub-field of economics. It was once separate from the economics of natural resources, but the two are now hard to tell apart. Its main professional bodies are the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists and the European Association for Environmental and Resource Economists.

nature-found-051.title: Scarcity: why there is never enough
nature-found-051.text: Air matters more to people than gold, yet gold is the scarce one. Producing air costs nothing, while gold must be found and processed. Scarcity is the basic fact that resources are limited, so only a limited amount of each good can be produced, while human wants have no such limit. There is never enough of something to satisfy every human want, even with advanced technology. Economists call a good scarce when more of it is wanted than is available at a price of zero. Scarcity is central to economic theory and is said to be essential to a proper definition of economics itself. It forces sacrifice: getting more of one thing means giving something else up, a trade-off. Market prices are one way to share out scarce resources. Some scarcity is made by people. Monopolies and stockpiling can create artificial scarcity, and panic buying can cause temporary scarcity. Some thinkers go further. They argue that scarcity comes not only from limited resources but also from human activity and the way societies provide for themselves.

nature-found-032.title: Negative externalities: the harm nobody pays for
nature-found-032.text: A neighbour's loud late-night music costs someone else a night's sleep. That lost sleep is a negative externality: a harmful side effect of producing or consuming something that lands on an unrelated third party. Its cost is not counted in the market price. It is also called an external cost or external diseconomy. Formally, it is the gap between what an action costs the person taking it and what it costs society. The music is a consumption example, but production causes them too. Air pollution from burning fossil fuels damages crops, materials, historic buildings and public health. Negative externalities are treated as more of a problem than positive ones. The reason is that they are inefficient in a strict sense: someone could be made better off without anyone being made worse off. That test of efficiency is explained in {{ref:nature-econ-168}}.

nature-found-084.title: Social cost: the full bill for an activity
nature-found-084.text: A driver pays the direct costs of a trip. Other people pay for the wear and tear, the congestion and the pollution the trip causes. Add the two together and you get social cost: the full cost of an activity to society. It is the private cost paid by those involved plus the external costs imposed on others who are not compensated. Private costs are the direct costs to the producer of making a good or service. When social costs exceed private costs, relying on private markets alone gives an inefficient result. The idea underlies efforts to price the harm from carbon emissions, explored in {{ref:nature-clim-241}}, which help judge policies such as a tax on carbon. How to close the gap is hotly debated. Pigou argued that government should tax each unit by the harm that one extra unit causes. Coase argued that the affected parties could bargain instead.

nature-found-037.title: Drawing an externality on a supply and demand graph
nature-found-037.text: Economists like to draw their problems. On the standard graph, one curve shows how much buyers want at each price and another shows how much sellers offer. The externality diagram adds an extra curve, to show how an externality pushes the market away from the best quantity for society. Take pollution from making steel. The private cost of making steel sits below its social cost, by the amount of the external cost. Buyers who count only private cost end up at a lower price and a higher quantity than the efficient one. People buy and use too much steel, and society would be better off if the extra units were never made. Efficiency requires producing only while the marginal social benefit, the gain to society from one more unit, exceeds the cost to society of that unit. An external benefit, such as vaccination, works the other way: the private benefit falls short of the social benefit. Competitive markets do not fix the gap. Some collective answer is needed, such as courts, bans or green taxes.

nature-found-033.title: Positive externalities: the bees that pollinate the neighbours
nature-found-033.text: A beekeeper keeps bees for honey. As a side effect, the bees pollinate the crops around them. That is a positive externality: a beneficial side effect of an activity that helps an unrelated third party, without that party paying for it. It is also called an external benefit or external economy, and it can come from production or consumption. Planting trees is another example: it makes nearby properties look nicer and cleans the surrounding area. Surprisingly, even positive externalities are a market failure, because the good ends up produced below the best amount. They invite free riding. A neighbour enjoying the bees for free has no reason to buy bees himself.

nature-found-040.title: Environmental valuation: reading nature's worth from behaviour and surveys
nature-found-040.text: When natural assets go unpriced, they tend to be both overused and underinvested in. Environmental valuation tries to correct this by putting an economic value on the environment and natural resources, many of which have no market price. Economists split these values in two. One kind comes from using nature, and it can be read from behaviour. The cost of recreational trips is one clue; house prices, in what are called hedonic methods, are another. The other kind comes from nature even when no one uses it. It includes the value of knowing nature exists and of keeping the option to use it later. It also includes the value of passing nature on, such as wanting to leave a pristine environment to one's children. These values are usually estimated with surveys. One survey method asks people what they would pay for an environmental benefit, or accept for its loss.

nature-found-039.title: Two schools: environmental and ecological economics
nature-found-039.text: Two schools study the same planet and often reach different conclusions. Environmental economics applies standard economics to the environment. The other, ecological economics, treats the economy as a part of the ecosystem. The split starts with training: most environmental economists trained as economists, while most ecological economists trained as ecologists. Ecological economists stress a "strong" form of sustainability. They reject the idea that human-made capital can stand in for natural capital. Their field is described as more pluralistic, open to many methods, and more focused on long-term sustainability and the scale of the economy. Environmental economics is seen as idealistic about the price system. The ecological school, by this account, is more realistic about factors outside it. The two schools hold conflicting views that trace back to different philosophical foundations, and the disagreement is unresolved.

nature-found-046.title: Ecological market failure: when the economy outruns nature
nature-found-046.text: Ecological economists make a bolder claim than most: the market cannot exist without "failing". Firms, they argue, routinely shift social and ecological costs onto others, including future generations. An ecological market failure is one in which economic activity exhausts vital resources that cannot be replaced, damages fragile ecosystems or overloads nature's ability to absorb waste. Today's prices cannot reflect the wishes of people not yet born, so finite minerals are not shared fairly over time, an issue called intergenerational fairness. Resources that renew themselves but that no one clearly owns get overused, as in too much fishing and grazing, a pattern explored in {{ref:nature-econ-606}}. Climate change is presented as an overwhelming example, with the atmosphere as a global common that no one owns. Growth becomes uneconomic when its ecological costs exceed its social benefits, a case explored in {{ref:nature-eecon-090}}. Herman Daly and Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen called for government limits on the overall level of economic activity. Ecological economists say most mainstream economists overlook these failures, because the standard test of efficiency ignores time.

nature-found-064.title: Government failure: when the fix falls short
nature-found-064.text: Government action meant to fix a market failure can itself fall short. Government failure is the economic waste that results, when an intervention leaves resources worse allocated than some available alternative. It happens when an intervention's costs outweigh its benefits, leaving society worse off than under another policy or none. It is about inefficiency, not about who wins and loses; simply creating winners and losers is not a government failure. Any form of intervention can fail: provision, taxes or subsidies, and regulation. Common mechanisms include regulators coming to serve the industries they oversee, unintended consequences, and inefficient outcomes that are easier politically than better ones. A small, well-organized interest group, for instance, can pressure lawmakers into policies that do not benefit society as a whole. The phrase became a term of art in the early 1960s. Coase used it in 1964, warning that all real social arrangements are more or less failures. Some economists argue that government failure can be worse than the market failure it targets.

nature-found-050.title: Does market failure even exist
nature-found-050.text: Not every economist accepts the idea of market failure. Arguments from several schools of thought call it misleading, too narrow, or no justification for government action. Some, such as Milton Friedman, argue that government failure may cost more than the market failure it tries to fix. Some Austrian School economists go further and deny that market failure exists. Entrepreneurs seeking profit, they say, remove inefficiencies on their own. Marxian economists take the opposite line: inefficient outcomes are built into capitalism, not rare exceptions. Inequality raises a different issue. High inequality is often called a market failure in everyday speech. Mainstream economics does not count it as one, because it is not Pareto inefficient: it can exist even when no one could gain without someone else losing. Zerbe and McCurdy add a final twist. Once the costs of making a trade are counted, market failure describes a situation that exists everywhere. The schools still disagree about whether market failure exists and whether it justifies government intervention.

nature-found-052.title: Absolute scarcity: Malthus and the limits of food
nature-found-052.text: In 1798 Thomas Malthus published his Essay on the Principle of Population. He argued that more food raises well-being only for a while, because population then grows. This view holds that population can grow exponentially, by multiplying, while food supply grows only linearly, by fixed steps. It is the root of absolute scarcity: a condition in which basic human needs, such as food, exceed the quantities of useful goods available. The economist Herman Daly describes absolute scarcity as the scarcity of resources in general. It rises as population and consumption approach the limit of what the biosphere can support. Substituting one resource for another eases absolute scarcity but cannot remove it, according to Daly. Malthus's view has dominated debate on hunger for two centuries, and it remains disputed.

nature-found-053.title: Relative scarcity: the reason economics exists
nature-found-053.text: Without scarcity, Paul Samuelson argued, there would be no economic goods at all. The kind of scarcity he meant is relative scarcity. It is a condition in which many different wants exceed the available means, which can be put to alternative uses, so people must choose. Mainstream economic theory stresses that it is relative scarcity that defines economics. Lionel Robbins put the point sharply. When time and means are limited and ends can be ranked, he argued, behaviour necessarily takes the form of choice. Every use of scarce means for one end gives up their use for another.

nature-found-036.title: Why externalities happen: ownership and the cost of trading
nature-found-036.text: Land and money are easy to own. Air, water and wild animals cross borders freely, so people use them without paying the full cost. One view holds that externalities come mainly from such poorly defined ownership rights, and from the costs of making trades. A person who gets a flu shot cannot own a share of the herd immunity it creates, so may skip it. The costs of making a trade also block some worthwhile exchanges; without them, people could bargain away every externality. The source itself flags this account as one-sided, calling it a narrow libertarian reading of Coase.

nature-found-038.title: Is environmental harm really an exception
nature-found-038.text: Karl William Kapp called the term "externality" a misnomer. Businesses, he argued, shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit. Ecological and heterodox economists, those outside the mainstream, build on this view. Clive Spash argues that fixing the odd externality leaves the deeper, system-wide problem untouched. Future generations, not yet born, cannot influence today's prices at all. These critics argue instead for a theory of social costs that prevents harm through precaution, an approach explored in {{ref:nature-pol-201}}. They dispute the mainstream view that pricing in externalities can correct environmental harm.

nature-found-035.title: Inframarginal externalities: side effects that change nothing
nature-found-035.text: Not every side effect distorts a market. An inframarginal externality is one that does not affect the marginal consumer, the buyer on the edge of deciding whether to buy at all. James Buchanan and Craig Stubblebine introduced the idea in 1962. Because it acts only away from the point where buyers and sellers settle, it does not misallocate resources. It causes no market inefficiency and needs no policy action.

nature-found-034.title: Positional externalities: keeping up with the neighbours
nature-found-034.text: When one member of a group buys a luxury car, the others may feel they must upgrade too. That pressure is a positional externality. In it, one person's purchase of a status good lowers the value others get from similar goods they already own. It grows from two ideas. Conspicuous consumption is buying to show off status. Positional goods are things whose value depends on comparison with what others own. The result can be a cascade of buying more than anyone needs, as people spend to keep their relative standing, wasting resources and widening inequality.

nature-found-085.title: Marginal social cost: the true cost of one more unit
nature-found-085.text: A steel firm decides how much to make by looking at its own costs. The cost it bears for one more unit is its marginal private cost. Marginal social cost adds the outside harm back in: it is the full cost to society of producing one more unit. Economists write it MSC = MPC + MEC, marginal private cost plus marginal external cost. With a negative production externality such as steel pollution, marginal social cost is greater than marginal private cost. Firms in a free market produce where marginal private cost meets marginal benefit, so they overproduce. The waste shows up as a loss to society, explored in {{ref:nature-econ-345}}. A tax equal to the damage from each extra unit raises private cost to match social cost. With a positive externality, such as research and development, there is underproduction, which a Pigouvian subsidy can correct. The rule is simple: production should rise only as long as the marginal social benefit exceeds the marginal social cost.

nature-found-041.title: Environmentally harmful subsidies: paying to use nature up
nature-found-041.text: Some government payments reward companies more for exploiting natural resources than for protecting them. The damage these environmentally harmful subsidies do to nature has been conservatively estimated at $4-$6 trillion U.S. dollars per year. The largest support the fossil fuel, agriculture and water sectors.

nature-found-043.title: The $7.3 trillion that industry never pays
nature-found-043.text: The world's largest industries burn through about $7.3 trillion of free natural capital per year. These are unpriced natural capital costs: the value of nature that industries use up without paying, which would change their profits if it were priced. Those industries would hardly be profitable if they had to pay for this damage. Cattle ranching and farming in South America ranks second. Its natural capital cost is 312.1 billion dollars, against revenue of just 16.6 billion.

nature-found-047.title: Failure of competition: when one firm holds the cards
nature-found-047.text: In a failure of competition, a firm or small group gains enough power over a market to block trades that would benefit both sides. This kind of market failure takes several forms: a market with a single seller, one with a single buyer, and markets where sellers compete with slightly different products. Such power can last where barriers to entry keep other firms out. An extreme case is natural monopoly, sometimes caused by extreme economies of scale, the cost advantages that come with sheer size.

nature-found-049.title: Unemployment and inflation as market failures
nature-found-049.text: Some market failures hit the whole economy at once. Unemployment, inflation and an economy thrown out of balance are seen as market failures at that scale. They can follow a financial crash, recession or depression. They show up as an economy producing below its capacity for a long time. Business cycles, the repeated downswings and upswings of an economy, are said to call for some government intervention.

nature-found-048.title: Unequal bargaining power: when one side can wait longer
nature-found-048.text: In many deals one side, such as an employer, can hold out longer than the other and so sets the terms. Unequal bargaining power is this kind of market failure. Since the early 20th century it has been used to justify rules protecting workers, consumers and tenants. Coase argued that it only shifts income from one side to the other. Behavioural evidence points the other way: unfair exchange lowers motivation to work, which makes it a real market failure.

nature-found-054.title: Three kinds of scarcity, and which ones cause conflict
nature-found-054.text: Scarcity comes in three kinds, and they do not all stir the same trouble. Demand-induced scarcity comes when demand for a resource rises while supply stays the same. Supply-induced scarcity comes when supply is very low compared with demand. It is mostly caused by environmental degradation, such as deforestation and drought. Structural scarcity arises when part of a population lacks equal access to resources, because of political conflict or location. Supply-induced and structural scarcity cause the most conflict within a country.

nature-found-086.title: Kapp's charge: capitalism as cost shifting
nature-found-086.text: Economist Karl William Kapp gave a blunt account of where social costs come from. In his heterodox view, outside the mainstream, they are the share of production costs that businesses shift onto society to raise profits. He blamed capitalist accounting laws that let producers leave these costs unpaid. On this view capitalism is essentially a system of cost shifting, and legal cost shifting is a main source of profit.

nature-found-087.title: Why social costs are so hard to count
nature-found-087.text: Pricing carbon means tracing a ton of heat-trapping gas through rising temperatures to crops, health, floods and ecosystems. That chain shows why social costs are hard to measure, especially future, environmental and long-range harms. Environmental, social and political harms that span long periods are hard to predict and put numbers on. So they are hard to include when weighing costs against benefits. Distance adds complexity: costs from one firm in China can affect people's health in the United States.

nature-found-074.title: Pecuniary externalities: side effects that work through prices
nature-found-074.text: City-dwellers who buy second homes in the countryside can push up house prices for local young people. That is a pecuniary externality: a side effect that works only by changing market prices, not by changing the real resources available to others. Technological or real externalities, such as factory pollution, harm others directly instead. In complete markets, buyers' losses from a price rise exactly match sellers' gains, so efficiency is kept. Some economists say these are not really externalities. When markets are incomplete or people face borrowing limits, they can matter, which helps justify macroprudential regulation of the financial system.

nature-found-088.title: The tyranny of small decisions: how marshes vanish plot by plot
nature-found-088.text: Between 1950 and 1970, almost 50 percent of the coastal marshlands of Connecticut and Massachusetts were lost. They went through hundreds of small conversions. Ecologist William Odum pointed this out in 1982, applying an idea called the tyranny of small decisions. It describes how many small decisions, each insignificant on its own, can add up to a large outcome that nobody chose or wanted. Economist Alfred E. Kahn introduced the idea in a 1966 essay and described it as a common route to market failure. His example was the passenger railway serving Ithaca. It was withdrawn because travellers' trip-by-trip choices did not cover its costs, though many would have paid to keep it. Each choice of one option over another is also a vote to remove the other option, which may then disappear. Lakes choked by excess nutrients, land turning to desert and the plight of most endangered species are said to stem from series of small decisions. One remedy is to build and protect higher levels of decision-making, from local to global, though these can push decisions back down.

nature-found-065.title: Why government fixes go wrong
nature-found-065.text: Governments find it hard to learn things such as production costs, so they may set quantities too high or too low. Missing information is one cause of government failure. Politics is another. Special interest groups can push politicians toward short-term gains. Critics say politicians favour quick, visible fixes over lasting long-term solutions, a political form of short-termism called policy myopia. Regulators who meet industry representatives often grow sympathetic, and write rules that favour producers over society.

nature-found-066.title: How taxes, subsidies and price controls bend markets
nature-found-066.text: Cap rents below the market price, and shortages follow. Set a wage floor above the market price, as a minimum wage does, and unemployment can follow. This is market distortion by government: the way taxes, subsidies and legal limits on prices change prices artificially and disturb how markets share out scarce resources. Subsidies can waste scarce resources by shielding inefficient firms from market forces. Taxes, meanwhile, give people a reason to evade them.

nature-found-090.title: A journal that explains environmental economics to everyone
nature-found-090.text: The Review of Environmental Economics and Policy is a peer-reviewed journal, checked by experts before publication, that appears twice a year. It is written to be readable by non-specialists. It is the official accessible journal of the Association of Environmental and Resource Economists. Its aim is to bridge academic research journals and the general press on environmental economics and policy.

nature-found-079.title: Pollution: nine million deaths and an unpaid bill
nature-found-079.text: In 2019 pollution killed about nine million people, about one in six of all deaths. Roughly three-quarters of them died from air pollution. Pollution is the release into the natural environment of contaminants that cause harm. It can be any substance, solid, liquid or gas, or energy such as heat, sound, light or radioactivity. The word usually means contaminants from human sources such as manufacturing, mining, poor waste management, transport or farming. Pollution can come from a point source, one concentrated site such as a factory, or a nonpoint source, spread out like farm runoff. Economists treat pollution from manufacturing as a negative production externality, imposing health and clean-up costs on all of society. Goods that pollute tend to be overproduced and underpriced, because the harm is not priced into the market. Polluting industries and waste sites are often placed near vulnerable and marginalized communities, a core reason for the movement for environmental fairness explored in {{ref:nature-gov-168}}. Many sources went unregulated during industrialization, until environmental regulation emerged in the later 20th century.

nature-found-075.title: Pollutants: when a substance becomes a problem
nature-found-075.text: Oil occurs naturally, yet it can still be a pollutant. A pollutant is a substance or form of energy put into the environment that has unwanted effects or makes a resource less useful. Some occur naturally; others are made by people, such as manufactured materials and by-products. A pollutant becomes pollution, or a health concern, once its concentration is high enough to do significant harm. It can then damage plant and animal growth, human health, resources people use, or property values. Some pollutants break down naturally. Others, such as the insecticide DDT, break down into products that are themselves pollutants. Measured against the planet's safe limits, mapped in {{ref:nature-eco-597}}, people have released novel entities, new kinds of substance, well beyond safe levels. Because pollutants cross borders, international rules are needed, such as the 2004 Stockholm Convention on persistent organic pollutants.

nature-found-055.title: Air pollution: 7 to 8 million deaths a year
nature-found-055.text: Air pollution kills 7 to 8 million people each year. It is the presence in the air of substances that harm people, other living things or the environment. The culprits may be gases, such as ozone or nitrogen oxides, or small particles, such as soot and dust, both outdoors and indoors. Tiny particles are its deadliest form. Outdoor pollution comes from burning fossil fuels for power and transport, wildfires, industry, waste, demolition and farming. Indoor pollution often comes from burning wood or crop waste for cooking and heating. The World Bank estimates its welfare and productivity losses cost the world economy over $8 trillion per year. Air pollution is a standard example of an externality: neither makers nor users of cars pay its cost to society. Many sources, especially fossil fuels, also release the heat-trapping gases that cause global warming. National laws have often worked, such as Britain's clean air law of 1956 and the 1963 US clean air law.

nature-found-067.title: Noise pollution: a hazard as old as ancient Rome
nature-found-067.text: Problems with urban noise are recorded as far back as ancient Rome. Noise pollution is sound that can harm the health of people and animals. Machines and transport are its main outdoor sources worldwide. Poor urban planning, such as industrial zones next to homes, brings it into residential areas. The burden is uneven: in the United States, noise is highest in low-income and racial minority neighbourhoods. For animals, noise can raise the risk of death by disrupting how they detect predators or prey. It can also interfere with breeding and navigation. In economic terms, a neighbour's loud late-night music causing lost sleep is a textbook negative consumption externality.

nature-found-057.title: The economic bill for dirty air
nature-found-057.text: In 2019, fine-particle pollution, known as PM2.5, cost the world economy over $8 trillion in health welfare costs, a World Bank study found. In India and China the loss was over 10% of GDP. About 85% of it came from lives lost, priced using a standard money value for lives, explained in {{ref:nature-val-019}}. These are the economic costs of air pollution: the losses it causes through ill health, lost work, lower crop yields and other damage. It also harms tourism, biodiversity, forestry and water quality. The OECD expects direct market costs from lost productivity, healthcare and crop losses to rise to 1% of GDP by 2060. Air pollution even cuts solar power, by blocking sunlight and dirtying panels.

nature-found-056.title: Air pollution and the body: 8.1 million deaths in a year
nature-found-056.text: Air pollution contributed to 8.1 million deaths in 2021, more than 1 in 8 deaths, according to the 2024 Global Burden of Disease Study. Breathing polluted air raises the risk of COPD, a long-term lung disease, as well as stroke, heart disease, lung cancer and pneumonia. Outdoor fine particles caused the most of these deaths, 4.7 million. Indoor particle pollution followed with 3.1 million, and ozone with 0.5 million. Burning fossil fuels is the largest source of air pollution deaths. In 2015, air pollution cut global average life expectancy by 2.9 years, against 0.3 years from all direct violence. Exposure in pregnancy makes stillbirth, miscarriage, birth defects and low birth weight more likely. Estimates differ by source: the World Health Organization puts the toll at 6.7 million deaths a year.

nature-found-072.title: Particulate pollution: no known safe dose
nature-found-072.text: There is no known safe level of exposure to particulate pollution: pollution made of tiny particles suspended in air, water or space. It takes three main forms: particles in the atmosphere, marine debris and space debris. Some particles are released directly, and others form by chemical reactions in the air, from natural or human sources. Sources include farming, cars, construction, forest fires and power plants. About 4.2 million premature deaths in 2016 were due to airborne particulate pollution, 91% of them in low and middle income countries. Rules can help. After tighter standards, US annual averages of fine particles, PM2.5, fell from 13.5 to 8.02 micrograms per cubic metre between 2000 and 2017.

nature-found-076.title: Stock and fund pollutants: what builds up and what fades
nature-found-076.text: Some pollution fades if emissions stay low enough, while some keeps piling up. A pollutant only causes pollution once the environment's assimilative, or absorptive, capacity is exceeded. That idea splits pollutants into two kinds. Stock pollutants, such as PCBs, non-biodegradable plastics and heavy metals, accumulate over time. The damage they do grows and persists. They burden future generations, with harm lasting long after the benefits are forgotten. Fund pollutants are absorbed if emissions stay low enough. Carbon dioxide, taken up by plants and oceans, is one example. Fund pollutants cause harm only when emissions outpace absorption. Even then they are not destroyed, but converted into less harmful substances or diluted.

nature-found-083.title: From ancient metalworking to London's Great Stink
nature-found-083.text: Greenland's ice holds a record of ancient industry. Ice cores drilled there show pollution rising with Greek, Roman and Chinese metal production. The Industrial Revolution then created pollution as it is known today. Responses came slowly. London's Great Stink on the Thames in 1858 led to the building of its sewer system. In 1881 Chicago and Cincinnati became the first American cities to pass clean air laws.

nature-found-082.title: Pollution control: better to prevent than to clean up
nature-found-082.text: Without pollution control, waste from farming, mining, manufacturing, transport and other activities would degrade the environment. Pollution control is the management of waste gases, liquids and other emissions released into air, water or soil. Its hierarchy of controls ranks the options. Preventing pollution and minimizing waste are preferred to controlling pollution afterwards. Devices include wastewater biotreaters, which use living organisms to clean water, and constructed wetlands.

nature-found-081.title: What it costs to cut pollution
nature-found-081.text: In 2005, US pollution abatement capital and operating costs came to nearly $27 billion. Abatement means cutting pollution, and its cost is what a firm pays to reduce the pollution it produces. Measured per extra unit cut, it is called marginal abatement cost. Firms cut pollution by choice, or because regulation forces them to.

nature-found-080.title: Why the best amount of pollution is not zero
nature-found-080.text: Society gets something from pollution: the polluting goods themselves, and lower prices. Otherwise no one would pollute. So the aim is not zero pollution but the socially optimal level, the amount at which society's welfare is greatest. That is where the harm of one more unit equals the benefit of producing it. The free market misses this point, because it ignores pollution's cost to society. The true supply curve sits higher than the market one, and the optimum lies where the curve of marginal social cost meets market demand. At that optimum, output is lower and price higher than in the free market, so the free market outcome is a market failure. A corrective tax proportional to the damage of each extra unit yields the efficient level of pollution reduction. The model is used to compare ways of internalizing the externality, such as tariffs, taxes on the damage like a carbon levy, and cap and trade. Accepting some pollution can raise overall wellbeing, though every increase is still a cost that must be counted.

nature-found-062.title: Air pollution laws: gaps around the world
nature-found-062.text: Some 43% of countries lack even a legal definition of air pollution. Another 34% lack outdoor air quality standards, and just 31% have laws on pollution from beyond their borders. Air pollution laws set limits on pollutant concentrations in the air, or on emissions from sources such as vehicles. Few countries set limits as strict as the World Health Organization recommends, and its advice is guidance, not binding rules. Internationally, the Montreal Protocol, ratified worldwide, succeeded, while climate action has been less successful.

nature-found-061.title: From black smoke as prosperity to cleaner air
nature-found-061.text: During the Industrial Revolution, coal burning raised outdoor pollution sharply. Yet city leaders saw black smoke as a sign of prosperity. Early laws against pollution were weak, because they were seen to clash with industrial interests. Disaster forced the turn. The Great Smog of London in 1952 killed some 12,000 people and led to a new clean air law in 1956. Later problems crossed borders. Acid rain needed international cooperation, and ozone-damaging chemicals were later phased out by negotiation.

nature-found-059.title: Primary and secondary pollutants: emitted or made in the air
nature-found-059.text: Carbon monoxide from car exhausts and sulfur dioxide from factories come straight from their sources. They are primary pollutants. Secondary pollutants form in the air, when primary pollutants react with each other or with the atmosphere. Ozone near the ground is one. Some pollutants are both, emitted directly and also formed from others.

nature-found-060.title: Ground-level ozone: the smog of hot afternoons
nature-found-060.text: Ozone near the ground peaks on hot summer afternoons. It forms mainly when nitrogen oxides and volatile organic compounds, carbon-based vapours, react in sunlight. Ground-level ozone is the main gas in photochemical smog, the haze that sunlight makes from these pollutants. It harms human health, materials, forests and crops, and it slows plants' capture of energy from sunlight. One study estimated that a 1% rise in ozone concentrations would cause a global economic loss of $10 billion each year.

nature-found-063.title: How dirty air shrinks harvests
nature-found-063.text: Cleaner air during India's COVID-19 lockdown boosted greenness and plant growth, most strongly in crops. The reverse is costly. Polluted air, especially ozone, cuts crop output and farm productivity. A 1% rise in PM2.5 levels would cause about $5 billion in losses, especially in colder climates. Pollution also lowers farm workers' productivity through its health effects.

nature-found-058.title: Who breathes the dirtiest air
nature-found-058.text: Polluting industries and roads are more often placed in poorer communities, whose residents also more often work outdoors. The result is unequal exposure: poorer groups and some racial groups breathe more polluted air than others. Low-income public housing residents, who cannot easily move, are heavily affected by nearby refineries and chemical plants. Children face more exposure too, because they breathe faster and closer to the ground.

nature-found-078.title: How much of a chemical is safe
nature-found-078.text: Industry keeps making new chemicals, and regulating them requires judging their danger to health and the environment. Risk assessment is now seen as essential for making these decisions on a scientific basis. It relies on pollutant risk thresholds: concentration levels used to decide how much of a chemical is safe. One is the no-observed-adverse-effect level, the highest dose at which no harm has been seen.

nature-found-077.title: Where pollutants do their damage
nature-found-077.text: Pollutants can be grouped by where they do damage, a scheme called zones of influence. Horizontally, local pollutants harm areas near the source, while regional pollutants harm areas further away. Vertically, surface pollutants build up near the ground, while global pollutants concentrate in the atmosphere.

nature-found-068.title: What noise does to the body
nature-found-068.text: An estimated 113 million people in Europe face road traffic noise above 55 decibels, the level at which noise becomes harmful. Unwanted sound harms both physical and mental health. It is linked to heart and circulation problems, high blood pressure, stress, tinnitus, a ringing in the ears, hearing loss and disturbed sleep. Long exposure above 85 A-weighted decibels, a scale adjusted to human hearing, can cause noise-induced hearing loss. Occupational hearing loss is one of the most common work-related illnesses in the US and worldwide.

nature-found-070.title: Measuring noise in decibels
nature-found-070.text: Road traffic and construction typically range from about 70 to over 100 decibels. Repeated exposure above about 85 dB raises the risk of hearing damage. Noise is measured as sound pressure levels in decibels, a logarithmic scale, in which each step multiplies rather than adds, linked to how people hear. Long-term community exposure is described with averaged measures, such as the equivalent continuous sound level and the day–night average sound level. The tools are sound level meters, or dosimeters worn by workers through a shift.

nature-found-071.title: Noise control: from nuisance to national policy
nature-found-071.text: Until the 1970s, governments tended to treat noise as a nuisance rather than an environmental problem. Many disputes are still settled by negotiation between the noise maker and the hearer. The US Noise Control Act of 1972 set a national policy against noise that endangers health and welfare. Noise control covers the rules and methods governments and communities use to limit harmful exposure. Building codes and local ordinances may set maximum noise levels for homes, businesses and industry. Noise barriers, speed limits, road surfaces and better planning reduce road noise.

nature-found-069.title: Whales change course: noise and wildlife
nature-found-069.text: Whales have changed their migration routes and calls to avoid human-made noise. Many animals rely on sound to communicate, find mates, navigate and avoid predators. Noise from traffic, ships and aircraft can reach undisturbed habitats and affect species' survival. At sea, human-made noise affects at least 55 marine species, and it is doubling every decade. It is now a prominent stressor on coral reefs, which communities depend on for fishing and tourism.

nature-found-073.title: PM10 and PM2.5: sizing up deadly dust
nature-found-073.text: Airborne particles come in two main size classes. PM10 covers coarse particles of 10 micrometres and smaller, and PM2.5 covers fine particles of 2.5 micrometres and smaller. A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. Fine particles can be breathed deep into the lungs and, with enough exposure, absorbed into the blood. Worldwide, PM10 at 70 micrograms per cubic metre and PM2.5 at 35 have been shown to raise long-term mortality by 15%. Older adults, children, pregnant women and people with weak immune systems face the greatest risk.

openers.why-markets-miss-nature: Economics studies how goods and services are produced, shared out and used, against the basic fact that resources are limited. Markets do much of that sharing, but sometimes they fail, and economic value is lost. Often the cause is an externality: a cost or benefit that lands on a third party and never shows up in the market price. Pollution is the textbook case, and this chapter follows it from definitions and diagrams to the argument over putting an economic value on nature.

reviews.why-markets-miss-nature: Markets share out scarce resources through prices, but prices leave out costs that land on others. Those externalities, from car exhaust to a neighbour's late-night music, lead markets to make too much of what harms and too little of what helps. Pollution shows the stakes: air pollution kills millions of people a year and costs the world economy over $8 trillion. Economists answer with taxes, valuation and standards, while critics warn that governments fail too and that firms shift costs onto others as a normal way of making profit. Ecological economists go further, arguing that today's prices cannot speak for people not yet born.
